title: CV, interviews and your first job
intro: A strong project portfolio can get you noticed, but your CV and interview performance still need to turn that attention into an offer. In this lesson, you will learn how to present your full-stack skills clearly, prepare for common interview stages, handle salary discussions and rejection, and approach your first 90 days with a professional mindset.
body:
## Your CV has one job

A junior developer CV does not need to prove that you know everything. Its first job is much simpler: **make the reader understand your profile quickly enough to want to talk to you**.

Recruiters often review large numbers of applications. Many companies also use an Applicant Tracking System, or ATS, to help filter and organize applications. You should therefore make your CV easy for both software and humans to parse.

For a junior full-stack developer, a one-page CV is usually a strong target. It forces you to focus on the evidence that matters most.

A practical structure is:

~~~text
Name + contact information

Short professional summary

Technical skills

Experience

Selected projects

Education / certifications
~~~

The exact order can vary depending on your experience, but the document should be easy to scan.

Avoid complicated layouts with multiple columns, text embedded in images, decorative charts, and unusual section names. A beautiful CV that an ATS cannot parse is not helping you.

## Write impact bullets

The strongest experience and project bullets describe an action, what you changed, and some evidence of the result.

~~~compare
{"left": {"title": "Duty", "lang": "text", "code": "Responsible for the backend of a\ncustomer portal.", "note": "Says what you were assigned, not what changed."}, "right": {"title": "Impact", "lang": "text", "code": "Built a Spring Boot + React customer\nportal that cut support emails by 40%\nfor 120 test users.", "note": "Action verb + what + measurable result."}}
~~~

A useful pattern is:

~~~text
Action verb + what you did + measurable result or scope
~~~

For example:

~~~text
Built a Spring Boot REST API for customer support tickets, reducing manual ticket tracking and supporting 500+ test records.
~~~

Or:

~~~text
Automated Docker-based integration testing with PostgreSQL, cutting local environment setup from several manual steps to one command.
~~~

Compare that with:

~~~text
Responsible for backend development.
Worked on the ticket system.
Helped with testing.
~~~

The second version tells the reader almost nothing. It describes responsibilities without showing what you actually accomplished.

Good bullets start with strong verbs such as built, designed, implemented, reduced, improved, automated, migrated, led, created, or delivered.

## Numbers make claims stronger

Numbers do not have to mean revenue. You can measure many aspects of software work:

- Number of endpoints.
- Number of users or records supported.
- Test coverage.
- Build or deployment time.
- Response-time improvements.
- Number of automated tests.
- Number of services.
- Time saved by automation.
- Number of screens or workflows.

For example:

~~~text
Implemented 12 REST endpoints for customer orders, invoices, and support tickets with JWT-based authorization.
~~~

If you do not have a meaningful real-world metric, do not invent one. Use a truthful measure of scope instead.

A statement such as “Built 15 automated integration tests covering customer ticket authorization” is useful because the number represents actual work.

## Tailor your CV to the job

One generic CV is convenient, but a tailored CV is usually more effective.

Start with the job advertisement. Identify:

- Required technologies.
- Important responsibilities.
- Experience level.
- Domain knowledge.
- Testing expectations.
- Cloud or DevOps requirements.
- Communication or collaboration requirements.

Then compare those requirements with your actual experience.

Suppose a job advertisement says:

~~~text
We are looking for a junior full-stack developer with Java, Spring Boot,
React, PostgreSQL, Docker and automated testing experience.
~~~

Your CV should make those skills easy to find if you genuinely have them.

You might move your customer portal project higher on the page and describe it as:

~~~text
Built a full-stack customer portal with React, TypeScript, Spring Boot and PostgreSQL, using Docker Compose and automated unit/integration tests.
~~~

Do not add technologies simply because they appear in the advertisement. Tailoring means **emphasizing relevant evidence**, not inventing experience.

## Use the CV Maker strategically

The site's CV Maker can help you turn your experience and projects into a structured CV. Treat it as a tool for producing a clear first version, not as a replacement for your judgment.

A good workflow is:

1. Collect your real experience and projects.
2. Identify the target role.
3. Select the technologies relevant to that role.
4. Write measurable, truthful bullets.
5. Generate or format the CV.
6. Read it as if you were the recruiter.
7. Remove anything that does not strengthen the application.
8. Export the final version and check its formatting.

The final CV should sound like you, not like a generic AI-generated candidate.

## Your portfolio and CV should reinforce each other

Your CV might say:

~~~text
Customer Portal — React, TypeScript, Spring Boot, PostgreSQL
Built a full-stack portal with authentication, order management and support tickets.
~~~

The portfolio should then provide the evidence behind that statement: screenshots, source code, architecture decisions, tests, and a live deployment where possible.

This creates a simple chain:

~~~text
CV claim
   ↓
Portfolio project
   ↓
GitHub repository
   ↓
Code + tests + documentation
~~~

The stronger that chain is, the easier it is for a technical reviewer to trust your claims.

## Where to apply

Do not limit yourself to one type of employer. For a junior full-stack developer, several routes can be useful.

In the Hungarian market, look at:

- Hungarian technology companies.
- Software consultancies.
- Product companies.
- Banks and financial technology teams.
- Telecommunications companies.
- Enterprise software organizations.
- Smaller companies with internal development teams.

Also consider remote EU roles where the employment arrangement allows it. Remote jobs can expand the market significantly, but competition is often higher and companies may have country-specific employment or contractor requirements.

Useful sources can include company career pages, LinkedIn, Hungarian job boards, specialist technology recruiters, and developer communities.

Do not apply only when the job description matches 100 percent of your experience. If you meet the core requirements and can realistically learn the missing parts, applying can be worthwhile.

At the same time, do not blindly send hundreds of identical applications. A smaller number of relevant, tailored applications can produce better results and gives you more opportunities to learn from the process.

## Understand the interview loop

A software engineering interview is usually a sequence of different conversations rather than one giant exam.

~~~diagram
{"type": "steps", "title": "A typical interview loop", "steps": [{"label": "Recruiter screen", "sub": "20–30 min · motivation, logistics"}, {"label": "Technical", "sub": "live coding or Q&A"}, {"label": "Take-home", "sub": "2–6 h · README matters"}, {"label": "Team / system design", "sub": "talk through trade-offs"}, {"label": "Offer", "sub": "negotiate calmly"}]}
~~~

A common process looks like:

~~~text
Application
   ↓
Recruiter screening
   ↓
Technical interview
   ↓
Coding task / take-home
   ↓
System design discussion
   ↓
Behavioural interview
   ↓
Offer
~~~

Not every company uses every stage. Some skip take-home assignments. Others combine technical and behavioural interviews. Senior positions may have much deeper system design discussions.

Your job is to understand what each stage is trying to measure.

## The recruiter screen

The first call is often about basic alignment rather than advanced algorithms.

You may be asked:

- Tell me about yourself.
- What kind of role are you looking for?
- Why are you interested in this company?
- What technologies do you work with?
- What is your availability?
- What are your salary expectations?
- Are you comfortable with the location or remote arrangement?

Prepare a concise introduction of around one or two minutes.

For example:

~~~text
I'm a full-stack developer focused on Java and Spring Boot on the backend and
React and TypeScript on the frontend. I've been building applications with
PostgreSQL, Docker and automated testing, and recently I've focused on a full-
stack customer portal that I designed and deployed end to end. I'm now looking
for a role where I can contribute to a production team while continuing to grow
as a software engineer.
~~~

Do not memorize this word for word. Understand the structure and make it natural.

## Technical interviews

Technical interviews vary significantly between companies.

You may be asked about:

- Java fundamentals.
- Object-oriented programming.
- Collections and generics.
- HTTP and REST APIs.
- Spring Boot.
- Spring Security.
- SQL and database design.
- React and TypeScript.
- Testing.
- Docker and deployment.
- Git.
- Basic algorithms and data structures.

Your preparation should focus on understanding concepts rather than memorizing definitions.

If asked why a database index can improve a query, you should be able to explain the trade-off. If asked what a JWT is, you should understand how it participates in authentication rather than simply knowing that it is “a token”.

The interview simulator on the site can help you practice explaining technical concepts under interview conditions. Use it actively: answer aloud, review weak areas, and repeat questions until your explanations become natural.

## Take-home assignments

A take-home task is an opportunity to demonstrate how you actually work.

Treat it like a small professional project.

Start by reading the requirements carefully. Then identify assumptions and write them down. Build the smallest complete solution before adding optional features.

A strong submission usually has:

- Clear setup instructions.
- Sensible project structure.
- Meaningful tests.
- Validation and error handling.
- Good naming.
- A useful README.
- Clean Git history.
- A clear explanation of trade-offs.

Do not spend twenty hours adding features that were not requested if the core requirements are incomplete.

## Light system design

A junior candidate is unlikely to be expected to design a global social network from scratch. However, you may be asked to explain how you would design a small application.

For the customer portal, you should be able to discuss:

~~~text
React frontend
      ↓
REST API
      ↓
Spring Boot services
      ↓
PostgreSQL
~~~

Then discuss authentication, authorization, validation, database relationships, error handling, logging, and deployment.

A useful system-design answer follows a simple progression:

1. Clarify the requirements.
2. Identify the main users and use cases.
3. Identify the main components.
4. Define the data model at a high level.
5. Define important API boundaries.
6. Discuss security and failure cases.
7. Mention scaling only where it is relevant.

Do not start by saying “we need Kubernetes and microservices.” Start with the problem.

## Behavioural interviews and STAR

Behavioural questions ask about how you work, communicate, solve problems, and handle difficult situations.

~~~diagram
{"type": "layers", "title": "STAR in one answer", "layers": [{"label": "Situation", "sub": "one or two sentences of context", "items": ["Our capstone demo failed the day before…"]}, {"label": "Task", "sub": "what you had to achieve", "items": ["Make the deploy reliable"]}, {"label": "Action", "sub": "what YOU did — the longest part", "items": ["added health checks", "rollback script"], "highlight": true}, {"label": "Result", "sub": "a number if possible", "items": ["0 failed deploys in 6 weeks"]}]}
~~~

The **STAR** structure is useful:

- **Situation:** What was happening?
- **Task:** What were you responsible for?
- **Action:** What did you actually do?
- **Result:** What happened afterward?

For example:

~~~text
Situation: A deployment was repeatedly failing because the local and CI environments differed.

Task: I needed to make the build reproducible.

Action: I containerized the required database setup and added the relevant configuration to CI.

Result: The team could reproduce the environment consistently and the deployment pipeline became more reliable.
~~~

The Action section should contain most of the useful detail. The interviewer wants to know what **you** did, not only what the team did.

Whenever possible, quantify the Result.

Instead of “The deployment became faster,” say “The deployment setup went from several manual configuration steps to one Docker Compose command.”

## Salary basics

Salary conversations can feel uncomfortable, especially for a first job. Prepare before the interview rather than improvising under pressure.

Research the market for the relevant:

- Country.
- City.
- Experience level.
- Technology stack.
- Company size.
- Employment arrangement.

Look at the complete compensation package, not only base salary. Depending on the employer, this can include bonuses, benefits, remote-work support, training budgets, private healthcare, equity, paid leave, or other benefits.

When asked for expectations, you can provide a range if you have researched a reasonable market position.

For example:

~~~text
Based on the role, my experience and the current market, I'm targeting a gross
monthly range of X to Y, depending on the overall compensation package and
responsibilities.
~~~

Know whether a figure is gross or net and whether it is monthly or annual. In international roles, understand whether compensation is an employee salary or contractor rate.

Do not choose a number solely because you are afraid that asking for more will end the conversation. At the same time, do not make unrealistic demands without evidence.

## Follow up professionally

After an interview, a short follow-up can be appropriate.

Thank the interviewer, mention something specific you found interesting, and reinforce your interest.

You do not need to write a long message. The purpose is professional communication, not persuasion at any cost.

If the recruiter gives you a timeline and the deadline passes, a polite follow-up is completely reasonable.

## Handling rejection

Rejection is part of the process, especially at the beginning of a career.

One rejection does not tell you that you are a bad developer. It might mean:

- Another candidate had more relevant experience.
- The company changed the role.
- The team needed a specific technology.
- Your interview answer was unclear.
- Your salary expectations did not align.
- There was simply a stronger candidate that day.

When possible, ask for feedback. You will not always receive it, but useful feedback can reveal patterns.

Track applications in a simple spreadsheet or board:

~~~text
Company | Role | Applied | Stage | Result | Feedback
~~~

After ten or twenty applications, patterns become visible. If applications rarely produce interviews, improve the CV and positioning. If interviews happen but offers do not, focus on interview preparation.

Treat the process as a feedback loop rather than a judgment of your identity.

## Your first 90 days

Getting the job is not the end of the learning process. Your first three months are an opportunity to establish trust.

### Days 1–30: Learn

Understand the product, architecture, team, development process, and deployment pipeline. Set up your environment. Read documentation. Ask questions. Learn how the team works.

Do not feel pressured to understand the entire system immediately.

### Days 31–60: Contribute

Start taking increasingly independent tasks. Fix bugs, implement small features, improve tests, and learn the team's review process.

Look for small wins that reduce friction without trying to redesign everything.

### Days 61–90: Own

Take ownership of a small area or workflow. Start identifying problems before someone assigns them to you. Explain your technical reasoning and communicate risks early.

The goal is not to prove that you are the smartest person on the team. The goal is to become someone the team can trust with real work.

## Common mistakes

### Sending the same CV everywhere

A generic CV makes relevant experience harder to find. Tailor the summary, skills emphasis, and strongest project bullets to the role.

### Listing skills without evidence

Anyone can write “Docker, Kubernetes, AWS, React, Java” on a CV. A project with Docker configuration, CI, deployment, and documented decisions is stronger evidence.

### Overclaiming

Do not describe yourself as an expert in technologies you have only used once. Interviewers can usually discover the difference quickly.

### Memorizing interview answers

Preparation is useful, but memorized answers often sound unnatural. Understand the concepts and practice explaining them in your own words.

### Solving the coding problem silently

During technical interviews, explain your thinking. Clarify assumptions, discuss trade-offs, and mention edge cases.

### Ignoring communication

Software development is collaborative. Technical ability without clear communication can become a serious weakness.

### Giving up after rejection

A job search is a process with noisy results. Measure where candidates are dropping out and improve that stage rather than assuming you need to rebuild everything.

## Your career loop

A sustainable early-career process looks something like this:

~~~text
Learn
  ↓
Build
  ↓
Document
  ↓
Publish
  ↓
Apply
  ↓
Interview
  ↓
Get feedback
  ↓
Improve
  ↓
Build again
~~~

Your capstone is not the final destination. It is your first strong piece of evidence that you can take a software problem from requirements through implementation and deployment.

Your CV gets that evidence in front of people. Your portfolio makes it easy to inspect. Your interview skills let you explain it. Your first job then gives you production experience that becomes the foundation for the next stage of your career.

The most important goal is therefore not to create a perfect candidate profile. It is to create a credible, honest and continuously improving one.
takeaways: Keep a junior CV concise, ATS-friendly, and focused on evidence.
Write bullets with action verbs, concrete work, and truthful metrics.
Tailor your CV to the actual requirements of each relevant role.
Prepare for interviews by understanding concepts and practicing explanations.
Use STAR to structure behavioural answers around your own actions and measurable results.
Treat rejection as feedback and use your first 90 days to build trust through learning, contribution, and ownership.

quiz.question: Which bullet is strongest for a junior full-stack CV?
options: Responsible for backend development.
Worked on various software projects.
Implemented 12 REST endpoints for customer orders and support tickets with JWT authorization.
Participated in development activities.
quiz.explanation: The third bullet starts with an action verb, describes concrete work, and includes a measurable scope.

quiz.question: What is the main purpose of tailoring a CV to a job advertisement?
options: To make the CV longer than one page.
To make relevant experience and skills easy to find for that particular role.
To include every technology mentioned in the advertisement regardless of experience.
To remove all project information.
quiz.explanation: Tailoring means emphasizing truthful, relevant evidence that matches the employer's requirements. It does not mean inventing experience.

quiz.question: What does the Action part of STAR describe?
options: What the candidate personally did to address the situation or task.
What the company planned to do in the future.
The final salary offered by the company.
The technical stack used by the whole team.
quiz.explanation: The Action part should explain the candidate's own contribution and decisions. This is particularly important when describing team situations.

quiz.question: What is a sensible approach to a junior system-design interview?
options: Immediately propose microservices and Kubernetes.
Focus only on database indexes.
Avoid discussing security because it is too advanced.
Clarify requirements first, then discuss components, data, APIs, security, and relevant trade-offs.
quiz.explanation: A strong junior system-design discussion starts with the problem and requirements before selecting architecture and discussing relevant technical concerns.

quiz.question: What is a useful goal for the first 30 days in a new development job?
options: Redesign the entire architecture.
Learn the product, team, development process, and technical environment.
Avoid asking questions to appear independent.
Immediately replace existing tools with your preferred ones.
quiz.explanation: The first month should primarily be about understanding the product, team, architecture, workflow, and development environment before taking on increasing ownership.

exercise.title: Review CV bullets and STAR answers
exercise.task:
Define exactly these two names: the top-level `const ACTION_VERBS` and the functions `reviewBullet(text)` and `starCheck(answer)`.

`ACTION_VERBS` must be exactly `['built','designed','implemented','reduced','improved','automated','migrated','led','created','delivered']`.

`reviewBullet(text)` must return `{ score, tips }`. Start the score at 0. Add 1 if the first word of the trimmed text, after stripping punctuation from that word and comparing case-insensitively, is in `ACTION_VERBS`. Add 1 if the text contains a digit. Add 1 if the trimmed text length is between 40 and 160 characters inclusive. Add 1 if the text does not contain `responsible for` or `worked on`, case-insensitively. For each missed point, add the corresponding message to `tips` in exactly this order: `Start with an action verb`, `Add a number that shows impact`, `Keep it between 40 and 160 characters`, `Avoid passive phrases like 'responsible for'`.

`starCheck(answer)` receives an object with `situation`, `task`, `action`, and `result` string properties, although any property may be missing. Return an array containing the names of missing or blank parts in this exact order: `situation`, `task`, `action`, `result`. If `result` is present and non-blank but contains no digit, also append `result needs a number` after the missing/blank parts. Do not add `result needs a number` when result is missing or blank.
exercise.hint: For `reviewBullet`, evaluate the four rules independently so that every failed rule can contribute its own tip. Strip punctuation only from the beginning and end of the first word before checking the action-verb list. For `starCheck`, iterate through the four parts in the required order and treat missing, non-string, and whitespace-only values as blank. Only add the numeric-result warning when the result is actually present and non-blank.

tests.name: It exports the required action verbs as a top-level constant
It gives full score to a strong action bullet
It accepts action verbs case-insensitively and strips punctuation
It reports every missed bullet criterion in the required order
It scores the four criteria independently
It treats length boundaries as inclusive
It detects passive phrases case-insensitively
It identifies all missing STAR parts in order
It accepts a complete STAR answer with a numeric result
It warns when a present result has no number
It handles missing properties and blank values safely
